name: Daria Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the night shift on line two at an industrial bakery, the one by the ring road that makes sliced bread and burger buns for the supermarkets. I start at ten at night, check the dough mixers, the divider, the prover, the big tunnel oven, then the slicer and the bagger at the end. If the dough's too wet or the oven drifts by five degrees, you lose a whole run, so most of my night is walking up and down, touching dough and reading the screens.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like my crew. Six of us, three languages, and we've got it down to a dance. What wears me out is the nights, and that the pay's a bit under what the big bakery two towns over pays, but that's a forty-minute drive. I see my kids at breakfast and that's about it on work days. Sami does the school runs, he drives a delivery van in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and a bit funny after all the fuss. In the break room I'd joke that the only AI we got was the one that writes the shift report wrong. Online I'd maybe share something about how the money should have gone to wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be okay with it. I use those chat tools now and then, mostly to translate safety notes for Nadia and Piotr, and that's useful. If that's all it ever is, fine. My worries are the night shifts and the bills, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Keep at the union about night-shift pay, because that's the real fight. Maybe ask for the day lead job when Ray retires next year, so I can see the kids more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat maybe, like a storm warning that turned into drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money should have gone to wages. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company spent a fortune last year on a new scheduling system with AI in it. It put me on four nights in a row with a day off in the middle, which is the worst thing you can do to a body. We went back to Ray's spreadsheet after two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the bill that worries you most right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage went up when our fixed rate ended, about a hundred and forty more a month. We're covering it by not saving at all. One car repair and we're on the credit card.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief and a bit funny after all the fuss. Online I might share something about how the money should have gone to wages instead.
S0.think: I'd honestly be fine with it. I use chat tools now and then to translate safety notes, and that's useful, but my real worries are night shifts and bills.
S0.do: Keeps leading the night shift and pushes the union on night-shift pay. Plans to apply for the day lead job when the current lead retires next year.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a warning that came to nothing.
S0.quote: It put me on four nights in a row with a day off in the middle, which is the worst thing you can do to a body.
S0.fieldNote: Daria's experience of AI so far is a failed scheduling system and a handy translation tool, which shapes a calm, practical view of the hype. Her stress is the mortgage rise and night shifts. She's clearly respected by a mixed-language crew and sees herself as their protector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, but the people who make the bread should be in the room when they decide what changes. At the union I'd ask for training on whatever comes in, paid, during shift hours. I'd say that to the managers too, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly watching and fixing. I think an AI could watch the oven better than me in a few years, and robots already stack trays in some plants. So my crew shrinks first, maybe from six to three, and I'm left minding machines. I could live with that if the pay's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good with the tools before they land, so I'm the one they pick to run the new system, not the one they let go. I'd sit with my daughter, she's fourteen and better at this than me, and practise in the evenings. And I'd back the union on a no-sackings deal, retraining for anyone moved off the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had something to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Piotr. He's on the slicer, he's sixty-one, and he's been told his whole life that he's not good with computers. If they move him to a screen job, he'll quit before he admits he's lost. I'd want to sit next to him on the training, not just send him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd practise with your daughter. What would that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday afternoons, kitchen table, her laptop. She'd show me how to ask the thing to explain an error code, and I'd show her what a proving cabinet is. We'd both learn something. She'd probably charge me for it.

S1.say: I'd say the people who make the bread should be in the room when changes are decided. At the union I'd ask for paid training on new systems during shift hours.
S1.think: I think AI could soon watch the oven better than me, and robots could stack trays, so my crew shrinks. I could live with minding machines if the pay's right.
S1.do: Learns the AI tools at the kitchen table with her daughter on Sundays so she's picked to run the new system. Backs the union on a no-sackings deal with retraining for anyone moved off the line.
S1.feel: Uneasy but with a sense of having something to do.
S1.quote: She'd show me how to ask the thing to explain an error code, and I'd show her what a proving cabinet is.
S1.fieldNote: Daria moves once she sees the change is real, but she moves with her people in mind. The image of Sunday lessons with her daughter was warm and specific. Her worry for Piotr shows she sees the human cost in pride as much as in pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency help, like during the pandemic. Pay people to stay home if the robots are cheaper, and make the companies pay for it. I'd be out on the street with the union, I'm not shy about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years? We're not ready. Sami's job driving the van goes too, probably before mine, because self-driving vans are already being tested. Two jobs gone in one house with less than a month saved. I don't know how we'd keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut straight away: no more takeaways, the kids' swimming stops, I'd sell the second car because Sami wouldn't need it. I'd talk to my mother about moving in with us, or us with her, which nobody wants. I'd sign up for every support scheme going and join every union action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. The kind of scared where you check your bank app at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two jobs in the house at risk. What would you and Sami actually say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami would say it'll be fine, he always does. I'd say, it won't be fine unless we make it fine. Then we'd sit at the kitchen table with the bills spread out and argue about which one to stop paying. Probably the phones, then the car insurance on the second car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina's fourteen, she'd be angry, at me, at the world. Theo's ten, he'd want to know if he can still do swimming. I'd tell them we'll be okay, which would be a lie, and they'd know it.

S2.say: I'd say we need emergency help like in the pandemic, with companies paying to support people whose work goes to robots. I'd be out on the street with the union.
S2.think: I think we're not ready at all. My partner's driving job could go before mine, and with two jobs gone and under a month saved, I don't know how we'd keep the house.
S2.do: Cuts takeaways and the kids' swimming, and sells the second car. Talks to her mother about moving in together, signs up for every support scheme and joins union action.
S2.feel: Scared enough to check the bank app at three in the morning.
S2.quote: The kind of scared where you check your bank app at three in the morning.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits Daria twice, because her partner's driving job is exposed too. She doesn't freeze; she makes a list, cuts, and looks to family, the state and the union. She was honest that reassuring her kids would be a lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly. Get the training money flowing now, and give the people who know the work first pick of the new jobs. I'd say it at work and I'd say it to whoever comes knocking before the election.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time for me to move, if I pick the right thing. I'd look at what's still standing when the robots come in: people who install and fix them, at least for a while. But I'd be fifty by then, and I'm not sure who hires a fifty-year-old trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course in industrial maintenance at the college, if the union or the company paid. I'd save whatever the overtime brings in, even if it's only a few hundred. Sami would look too, maybe at the hospital, since they'll still need porters for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. Like I've got a map, even if it's a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier your evenings are for sleep before nights. When would you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that's the problem. I'd have to get off nights first, which means getting Ray's day lead job. Then two evenings a week at college. If I don't get the day job, the plan falls apart, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to finish a course and get my first job in the new thing before the wave hits. With two years, I'd be scrambling for whatever's left. With five, I might be one of the people fixing the robots that replaced my crew, which is a strange thought.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so get the training money flowing now and give people who know the work first pick of new jobs. I'd tell that to anyone canvassing before the election.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to move if I choose well, perhaps to installing and fixing robots. But I'd be fifty and unsure who hires a fifty-year-old trainee.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening industrial maintenance course in the first year if the union or company pays, which depends on moving to the day lead job. Saves overtime money, and her partner looks at hospital jobs.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control, like having a map, even a bad one.
S3.quote: With five, I might be one of the people fixing the robots that replaced my crew, which is a strange thought.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Daria from defence to a plan, but the plan hangs on one step: getting off nights. She was quick to admit the weak point when I asked about it. She feels the strangeness of fixing the robots that replace her crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if anyone in charge actually wants to. I'd push for a plan where nobody's dropped, like a pension bridge for older workers and real training for the rest. I'd also vote for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years from now I'm fifty-three. I'd get one more career in, maybe. I keep thinking, though: if AI can do almost any work, then the course I take is just a stop on the way. I'd still do it, because doing nothing is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the day lead job and start the maintenance course. Over the next few years I'd try to pay the credit card down and keep a small pot. With Lina, I'd be pushing her to think about something with caring or teaching, things where people want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, but less raw. It's more like a long job you know you have to finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the course is just a stop on the way. Why do it then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a stop on the way still pays the mortgage for a few years. And because I'd go mad watching it happen with my arms folded. My mum always said you don't stand still when the floor's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lina when she asks what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn something useful and to keep learning. And to join a union wherever she goes, because nobody's going to look after you if you don't look after each other.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly if those in charge want to. I'd push for a plan where nobody's dropped, with a pension bridge for older workers and real training for the rest.
S4.think: I think I'd get maybe one more career at fifty-three. If AI can do almost any job, any course is just a stop on the way, but doing nothing would be worse.
S4.do: Moves to the day lead job and starts a maintenance course in the first year, then pays down the credit card over the following years. Steers her daughter toward caring or teaching work and votes for a fair transition plan.
S4.feel: Still worried but less raw, like a long job she knows she has to finish.
S4.quote: My mum always said you don't stand still when the floor's moving.
S4.fieldNote: Daria's long-horizon plan is the same as the five-year one, done with less panic. She's clear that retraining may only buy a few years, and does it anyway out of a sense of duty to herself and her family. Her advice to her daughter mixes skills with solidarity.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits Sami and me at the same time. What would help is income support that kicks in straight away, not after six months of forms, and paid training that fits around shift work. And somebody who understands that night-shift workers can't go to a nine-to-five course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who looks after the kids while we all retrain. That's the bit nobody plans for. Everybody talks about courses, nobody talks about who's home at seven when Theo needs dinner.

headlineQuote: Everybody talks about courses, nobody talks about who's home at seven when Theo needs dinner.
portrait: Daria Petrov is a 43-year-old night-shift lead at an industrial bakery, running a six-person, three-language crew on a bread line. She uses AI tools now and then, mostly to translate safety notes, and her partner Sami drives a delivery van. She's calm about the AI Plateau and only a little uneasy about Steady Disruption, where she plans to learn the tools with her daughter. AGI in 2 years alarms her because both household jobs are exposed and they have under a month saved, while 5 or 10 years gives her time for a maintenance course if she can get off nights. Throughout she backs the union and public support, and keeps thinking about the older crew members who'd struggle most.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her job and her partner's driving job at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts straight away without months of forms, and paid training that fits around shift work and childcare.
